Conclusions Thisstudyaddressedthefundamentalchallengeofmitigatingtrafficoscillationsinmixedtrafficflow:theinherent conflictbetweentheneedforhigh-fidelity,nonlinearmodelsofHDVbehaviorandtherequirementforcomputationally tractable,linearmodelsforreal-timeMPC.Toresolvethis,weproposedanovelframeworkbasedonKoopmanoperator theory, which successfully decouples modeling complexity from control complexity. Our proposed deep Koopman network,AdapKoopnet,demonstrateditscapabilitytolearncomplex,personalizeddrivingbehaviorsfromnaturalistic data,autonomouslyidentifyinglatenttrafficscenariosanddrivercharacteristicswithoutpre-definedlabels.Itssuperior Hao Lyu et al.: PreprintsubmittedtoElsevier Page 26 of 29 multi-steppredictionperformance,whichsurpassesthatoftraditionalnonlineardeeplearningmodels,providedthe foundationforourcontrolstrategy. The resulting AdapKoopPC framework integrates these learned, high-dimensional linear models into an MPC scheme,creatingascalableandadaptivecontrolarchitectureforCAVs.Extensivesimulationsvalidatedtheefficacy of this approach. In both small- and large-scale mixed traffic systems, AdapKoopPC significantly attenuated traffic oscillations and enhanced traffic stability, proving effective even at low CAV penetration rates of 10-20%. The frameworkdemonstratedrobustnessacrossvariousCAVdistributionsandunderdegradedcommunicationconditions, allwhilemaintainingremarkablecomputationalefficiencysuitableforreal-timedeployment.Thisworkconfirmsthat the proposed Koopman-based data-driven predictive control paradigm offers a powerful and practical solution for smoothingmixedtrafficflow. Despite these promising results, this study has limitations that open avenues for future research. The current AdapKoopnet relies on offline training and does not support online updates, which could be critical for adapting to non-stationary driving behaviors. Moreover, the scalability of the centralized MPC in AdapKoopPC may still face challenges in ultra-large-scale systems. Future work will focus on developing online learning mechanisms for the Koopman operator and exploring efficient distributed control architectures to further enhance the framework’s applicabilitytocomplex,real-worldtrafficenvironments,includingmulti-lanescenarios. JSON: Name: adapkooppc Title: Adaptive deep Koopman predictive control for mitigating traffic oscillations in mixed autonomous and human-driven vehicle flow Short Hypothesis: Embedding an adaptively learned deep Koopman linear predictor that conditions on latent driving-scenario features into an MPC controller reduces mixed-traffic velocity and headway oscillation metrics (velocity RMSE and headway RMSE or standard deviation) by a statistically significant margin compared to non-adaptive Koopman, black-box nonlinear predictors, and model-mismatch linear MPC baselines at CAV penetration rates up to 20%. Related Work: Existing approaches to mitigate traffic oscillations fall into three families: physics-based car-following models with analytic controllers, data-driven black-box predictors coupled with control, and non-parametric/data-enabled predictive control. Physics-based models are interpretable and computationally light but suffer from systematic mismatch to real driving heterogeneity. Black-box deep predictors (e.g., LSTM) capture nonlinear, heterogeneous HDV behavior but yield nonconvex models that are expensive or unsuitable for real-time constrained optimization. Non-parametric predictive control frameworks avoid explicit dynamics but require large representative datasets and incur high online computational cost that scales poorly. Prior Koopman-based methods provide linear predictive cores but are typically trained as monolithic operators for fixed platoon configurations or synthetic simulation data, lack scenario-adaptive conditioning and validation on naturalistic heterogeneous trajectories, and do not address dynamic reconfiguration for arbitrary local mixed-traffic compositions. Abstract: Mixed traffic containing connected automated vehicles (CAVs) and human-driven vehicles (HDVs) produces stop-and-go oscillations that reduce safety and efficiency. We propose Adaptive Deep Koopman Predictive Control (AdapKoopPC): a pipeline that trains a deep Koopman network to extract latent driving-scenario-conditioned representations from unlabeled trajectory context and learns a finite-dimensional linear evolution operator and linear decoder in the lifted space. The learned linear predictor is embedded directly into a model predictive control optimizer, enabling convex quadratic programming for real-time actuation of CAVs while preserving high-fidelity, personalized HDV prediction. Core contributions are (1) a scenario-aware deep Koopman predictor that captures heterogeneous driver characteristics from naturalistic trajectories, (2) a design to produce a computationally tractable linear predictive core compatible with MPC constraints, and (3) a scalable procedure to assemble local predictive models for arbitrary CAV/HDV mixes. Expected outcomes are reduced velocity and headway oscillation amplitudes and solver runtimes competitive with or better than nonlinear data-driven alternatives, particularly at low-to-moderate CAV penetration. Experiments: Datasets: use a large naturalistic highway trajectory dataset (all available segments matching car-following conditions) partitioned into train/val/test splits; simulation environment for mixed-traffic validation replicating stop-and-go leader disturbance with parameterized platoons (small-scale N=10 and large-scale N=50). Baselines: (1) LTI-MPC with calibrated physics-based car-following model, (2) black-box predictor (LSTM) + nonlinear MPC, (3) non-parametric DeeP-LCC style predictive controller, (4) Koopman predictor without scenario-adaptive feature extraction + MPC. Metrics: prediction RMSE for velocity and headway over multi-step horizons, system-level velocity standard deviation, headway standard deviation, peak acceleration magnitude, control solver wall-clock latency per control step, and statistical significance (paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05). Training and inference settings: sample interval Δt=0.12s, prediction horizon 15 steps (1.8s), control horizon 10 steps; train deep models with identical embedding dimensionality sweeps (e.g., 64, 128, 256) and fixed training epochs and batch size; use identical MPC weighting matrices across controllers. Ablations: (A1) remove driving-scenario semantic extraction from deep Koopman network, (A2) replace linear decoder with nonlinear decoder while keeping Koopman evolution, (A3) vary Koopman lifted dimension, (A4) vary CAV penetration rates {0%,10%,20%,30%}. Evaluation protocol: report mean and 95% CI across ≥30 randomized initial seeds for each condition, perform pairwise statistical tests against each baseline, and present computational profiles (mean and max solver time). Risk Factors and Limitations: Offline training mismatch to non-stationary driving behavior and distributional shift; limited generalization from highway-only naturalistic data to urban, multi-lane, or intersection scenarios; inability of a finite-dimensional Koopman truncation to capture all relevant nonlinear modes leading to biased predictions and unsafe control actions; degraded performance under frequent lane changes or unobserved interactions; dependence on accurate measurements of preceding-vehicle future velocities for prediction inputs in the proposed formulation; sensitivity to sensor noise and communication loss or latency; scalability limits of centralized MPC as system size grows and associated solver time increases; potential numerical ill-conditioning of learned Koopman matrices affecting stability of long-horizon prediction; dataset selection bias (regional driving styles) limiting transferability; safety-critical constraint violations if model error is underestimated during optimization.
